claim: Cohesin folds chromosomes via DNA loop extrusion.
source: Cohesin folds chromosomes via DNA loop extrusion.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cohesin function.

claim: Cohesin-mediated chromosome loops regulate transcription by shaping long-range enhancer–promoter interactions.
source: Cohesin-mediated chromosome loops regulate transcription by shaping long-range enhancer–promoter interactions, among other mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cohesin function.

claim: Mutations of cohesin subunits and regulators cause human developmental diseases termed cohesinopathy.
source: Mutations of cohesin subunits and regulators cause human developmental diseases termed cohesinopathy.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cohesinopathy.

claim: Vertebrate cohesin consists of SMC1, SMC3, RAD21, and either STAG1 or STAG2.
source: Vertebrate cohesin consists of SMC1, SMC3, RAD21, and either STAG1 or STAG2.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cohesin composition.

claim: Stag2 cKO mice exhibit growth retardation, neurological defects, and premature death.
source: Stag2 cKO mice exhibit growth retardation, neurological defects, and premature death, in part due to insufficient myelination of nerve fibers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of the Stag2 cKO mice phenotype described in the manuscript.

claim: Stag2 cKO mice exhibit insufficient myelination of nerve fibers.
source: Stag2 cKO mice exhibit growth retardation, neurological defects, and premature death, in part due to insufficient myelination of nerve fibers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and histological analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stag2 cKO oligodendrocytes exhibit delayed maturation.
source: Stag2 cKO oligodendrocytes exhibit delayed maturation and downregulation of myelination-related genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq and trajectory analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stag2 cKO oligodendrocytes exhibit downregulation of myelination-related genes.
source: Stag2 cKO oligodendrocytes exhibit delayed maturation and downregulation of myelination-related genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing reduced expression of myelination genes.

claim: Stag2 loss reduces promoter-anchored loops at downregulated genes in oligodendrocytes.
source: Stag2 loss reduces promoter-anchored loops at downregulated genes in oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: STAG2-cohesin generates promoter-anchored loops at myelination-promoting genes to facilitate their transcription.
source: Thus, STAG2-cohesin generates promoter-anchored loops at myelination-promoting genes to facilitate their transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of Hi-C and RNA-seq data showing correlation between loop reduction and gene downregulation.

claim: Defective myelination is a contributing factor to cohesinopathy.
source: Our study implicates defective myelination as a contributing factor to cohesinopathy and establishes oligodendrocytes as a relevant cell type to explore the mechanisms by which cohesin regulates transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic and molecular data from Stag2 cKO mice.

claim: Oligodendrocytes are a relevant cell type to explore the mechanisms by which cohesin regulates transcription.
source: Our study implicates defective myelination as a contributing factor to cohesinopathy and establishes oligodendrocytes as a relevant cell type to explore the mechanisms by which cohesin regulates transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings that oligodendrocytes show clear transcriptional and chromosomal loop defects upon Stag2 loss.

claim: Cohesin was initially discovered as the molecular glue that tethers sister chromatids for segregation during mitosis.
source: Initially discovered as the molecular glue that tethers sister chromatids for segregation during mitosis (Haarhuis et al., 2014; Uhlmann, 2016; Yatskevich et al., 2019; Zheng and Yu, 2015), the cohesin complex has later been shown to be critical for structured chromosome folding and gene expression (Haarhuis et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cohesin complex is critical for structured chromosome folding and gene expression.
source: Initially discovered as the molecular glue that tethers sister chromatids for segregation during mitosis (Haarhuis et al., 2014; Uhlmann, 2016; Yatskevich et al., 2019; Zheng and Yu, 2015), the cohesin complex has later been shown to be critical for structured chromosome folding and gene expression (Haarhuis et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cohesin is loaded on chromosomes by the cohesin loader NIPBL.
source: Cohesin is loaded on chromosomes by the cohesin loader NIPBL.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cohesin loading.

claim: The cohesin–NIPBL complex can extrude DNA loops bidirectionally in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: The cohesin–NIPBL complex can extrude DNA loops bidirectionally in an ATP-dependent manner (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Vian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CTCF has been proposed to block loop extrusion by cohesin, establishing topologically associated domains (TADs) and marking TAD boundaries.
source: The chromatin insulator CTCF has been proposed to block loop extrusion by cohesin, establishing topologically associated domains (TADs) and marking TAD boundaries.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about CTCF function.

claim: Chromatin interactions within each TAD are favored whereas inter-TAD interactions are disfavored.
source: Chromatin interactions within each TAD are favored whereas inter-TAD interactions are disfavored.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about TAD properties.

claim: Chromosome loops and TADs shape long-range cis–element interactions, such as promoter–enhancer interactions, thereby regulating transcription.
source: Thus, chromosome loops and TADs shape long-range cis–element interactions, such as promoter–enhancer interactions, thereby regulating transcription.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about how chromosome structure regulates transcription.

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 bind to RAD21 in a mutually exclusive manner.
source: STAG1 and STAG2 bind to RAD21 in a mutually exclusive manner and create docking sites for several regulatory proteins, including CTCF (Hara et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 create docking sites for several regulatory proteins, including CTCF.
source: STAG1 and STAG2 bind to RAD21 in a mutually exclusive manner and create docking sites for several regulatory proteins, including CTCF (Hara et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 interact with DNA and the SMC1–SMC3 hinge domains.
source: STAG1 and STAG2 also interact with DNA and the SMC1–SMC3 hinge domains (Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 play redundant roles in sister-chromatid cohesion in cultured human cells.
source: STAG1 and STAG2 play redundant roles in sister-chromatid cohesion in cultured human cells, as both need to be simultaneously depleted to produce overt cohesion defects (Hara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutations of NIPBL and cohesin subunits, including STAG2, result in human developmental diseases termed cohesinopathies.
source: Mutations of NIPBL and cohesin subunits, including STAG2, result in human developmental diseases termed cohesinopathies, which affect multiple organs and systems (Remeseiro et al., 2013b; Soardi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In patients with cohesinopathies, mental retardation and neurological abnormalities caused by brain development defects are common.
source: In patients with cohesinopathies, mental retardation and neurological abnormalities caused by brain development defects are common (Piché et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of gene transcription as a result of reduced cohesin functions has been suggested to underlie developmental defects in cohesinopathy.
source: Dysregulation of gene transcription as a result of reduced cohesin functions has been suggested to underlie these developmental defects (De Koninck and Losada, 2016; Remeseiro et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several cohesin genes, including STAG2, are frequently mutated in a variety of human cancers.
source: In addition, several cohesin genes, including STAG2, are frequently mutated in a variety of human cancers (Martincorena and Campbell, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Stag1 is required for mammalian embryonic development.
source: Stag1 is required for mammalian embryonic development (Remeseiro et al., 2012), indicating that Stag2 cannot compensate for the loss of Stag1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Stag2 cannot compensate for the loss of Stag1 during mammalian embryonic development.
source: Stag1 is required for mammalian embryonic development (Remeseiro et al., 2012), indicating that Stag2 cannot compensate for the loss of Stag1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited finding that Stag1 is required for development.

claim: A Stag2 'floxed' mouse line (Stag2f/f) was created by homologous recombination with a template that contained two LoxP sites flanking exon 8.
source: To examine the physiological functions of Stag2 in the mouse, we created a Stag2 'floxed' mouse line (Stag2f/f) by homologous recombination with a template that contained two LoxP sites flanking exon 8 (Figure 1A, B) and targeted a critical exon (exon 8) of Stag2, which is located on the X chromosome, using CRISPR–Cas9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental description and Figure 1A, B.

claim: Exon 8 of Stag2 is a critical exon located on the X chromosome.
source: To examine the physiological functions of Stag2 in the mouse, we created a Stag2 'floxed' mouse line (Stag2f/f) by homologous recombination with a template that contained two LoxP sites flanking exon 8 (Figure 1A, B) and targeted a critical exon (exon 8) of Stag2, which is located on the X chromosome, using CRISPR–Cas9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the experimental description.

claim: Stag2null embryos showed severe developmental defects and underwent necrosis by E11.5 days.
source: The Stag2null embryos showed severe developmental defects and underwent necrosis by E11.5 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Stag2 is required for mouse embryonic development.
source: Thus, Stag2 is required for mouse embryonic development, consistent with a previous report (De Koninck et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Stag2null embryos die early, and is supported by a citation.

claim: Stag1 and Stag2 have nonredundant developmental functions.
source: Stag1 and Stag2 have nonredundant developmental functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both Stag1 and Stag2 are individually required for development.

claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre pups presented growth retardation and premature death.
source: The progenies were born in the Mendelian ratio, but Stag2f/y;NesCre pups presented growth retardation and premature death (Figure 1E, G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1E, G.

claim: More than 50% Stag2f/y;NesCre mice died aged about 3 weeks while the rest died at about 4 months.
source: More than 50% Stag2f/y;NesCre mice died aged about 3 weeks while the rest died at about 4 months.
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stag2f/y mice did not show differences discernible from wild-type (WT) littermates.
source: Stag2f/y mice did not show differences discernible from wild-type (WT) littermates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice exhibited frequent hydrocephaly.
source: Although Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not present microcephaly, they exhibited frequent hydrocephaly that might contribute to their premature death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Hydrocephaly might contribute to premature death in Stag2f/y;NesCre mice.
source: Although Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not present microcephaly, they exhibited frequent hydrocephaly that might contribute to their premature death.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of hydrocephaly.

claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice displayed normal drinking and feeding behaviors.
source: The Stag2f/y;NesCre mice displayed normal drinking and feeding behaviors (Figure 1H), but showed reduced plasma IGF-1 levels compared to the control mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic cage analysis data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed reduced plasma IGF-1 levels compared to control mice.
source: The Stag2f/y;NesCre mice displayed normal drinking and feeding behaviors (Figure 1H), but showed reduced plasma IGF-1 levels compared to the control mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by IGF-1 measurement data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping.
source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping (Figure 1K) and limb tremors (Video 1), which were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1K.

claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed limb tremors.
source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping (Figure 1K) and limb tremors (Video 1), which were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Video 1.

claim: Forepaw and hindlimb clasping and limb tremors were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed forepaw and hindlimb clasping (Figure 1K) and limb tremors (Video 1), which were not seen in Stag2f/y mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Stag2 deficiency in the nervous system causes growth retardation and neurological defects.
source: These data indicate that Stag2 deficiency in the nervous system causes growth retardation and neurological defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic observations of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice.

claim: H&E staining of brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not reveal overt anatomical defects.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice did not reveal overt anatomical defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The differentiation of neurons and astrocytes in Stag2-deleted brains was largely normal.
source: As revealed by immunohistochemistry assays using neuron- or astrocyte-specific antibodies, the differentiation of neurons and astrocytes in Stag2-deleted brains was largely normal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: 105 genes were significantly downregulated by more than twofolds in Stag2-deficient brains at post-natal day 21.
source: Compared with the control groups, 105 and 62 genes were significantly down- or upregulated by more than twofolds, respectively, in the Stag2-deficient brains.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claim: 62 genes were significantly upregulated by more than twofolds in Stag2-deficient brains at post-natal day 21.
source: Compared with the control groups, 105 and 62 genes were significantly down- or upregulated by more than twofolds, respectively, in the Stag2-deficient brains.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claim: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs in the brains of Stag2 cKO mice, 44 were enriched in myelin.
source: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs in the brains of Stag2 cKO mice, 44 were enriched in myelin (Figure 2C; Thakurela et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis and comparison with myelin-enriched gene lists from previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol biosynthesis pathways are the most affected canonical pathways in Stag2 cKO brains.
source: The ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) pinpoints cholesterol biosynthesis pathways as the most affected canonical pathways (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cholesterol biosynthesis precursors were reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
source: We further confirmed that the cholesterol biosynthesis precursors were reduced in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Myelin is the membrane sheath that wraps around axons to facilitate rapid nerve conduction and maintain metabolic supply.
source: Myelin is the membrane sheath that wraps around axons to facilitate rapid nerve conduction and maintain metabolic supply (Williamson and Lyons, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Dynamic myelination in the central nervous system (CNS) is critical for proper neurodevelopment.
source: Dynamic myelination in the central nervous system (CNS) is critical for proper neurodevelopment, and defective myelination is associated with autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases (Mathys et al., 2019; Wolf et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Defective myelination is associated with autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Dynamic myelination in the central nervous system (CNS) is critical for proper neurodevelopment, and defective myelination is associated with autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases (Mathys et al., 2019; Wolf et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cholesterol biosynthesis is essential for normal myelination.
source: Cholesterol biosynthesis is essential for normal myelination (Hubler et al., 2018; Saher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed greatly reduced luxol fast blue (LFB) staining compared to those of Stag2f/y and NesCre heterozygous mice at about P21.
source: Indeed, brain sections of Stag2f/y;NesCre mice showed greatly reduced luxol fast blue (LFB) staining compared to those of Stag2f/y and NesCre heterozygous mice at about P21 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by LFB staining data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Stag2 cKO mice had significant defects in myelin fiber formation at P18-P21.
source: Immunohistochemistry using antibodies against myelin proteins, Myelin basic protein (MBP) and Proteolipid protein 1 (PLP1), confirmed that Stag2 cKO mice had significant defects in myelin fiber formation at P18-P21 (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B–F.

claim: In both cerebral cortex and cerebellum, there were fewer and sparser myelin fibers in Stag2f/y;NesCre mice, as compared to the Stag2f/y controls.
source: In both cerebral cortex and cerebellum, there were fewer and sparser myelin fibers in Stag2f/y;NesCre mice, as compared to the Stag2f/y controls.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and quantification data.

claim: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice at P18 had significantly fewer myelin-wrapped axons at optic nerves.
source: Stag2f/y;NesCre mice at P18 had significantly fewer myelin-wrapped axons at optic nerves.
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Myelination predominantly occurs at 3 weeks after birth in the mouse.
source: Myelination predominantly occurs at 3 weeks after birth in the mouse.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The timing of premature death of Stag2 cKO mice is consistent with defective myelination as a contributing factor to the lethality.
source: The timing of premature death of Stag2 cKO mice is thus consistent with defective myelination as a contributing factor to the lethality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between the timing of myelination and the timing of death.

claim: Both Stag1 and Stag2 were expressed at high levels in hippocampus, medial habenula, neocortex, and cerebellum granular layer.
source: Both Stag1 and Stag2 were expressed at high levels in hippocampus, medial habenula, neocortex, and cerebellum granular layer.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Stag2 transcripts were detected at relatively high levels in subventricular zone, thalamus, fiber tracts, midbrain, and hindbrain regions.
source: Aside from these regions, the Stag2 transcripts were detected at relatively high levels in subventricular zone, thalamus, fiber tracts, midbrain, and hindbrain regions.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Stag2 is ubiquitously expressed in the brain.
source: Stag2 is thus ubiquitously expressed in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in situ hybridization data showing widespread expression.

claim: Oligodendrocytes (OLs) are responsible for myelination in the CNS.
source: Oligodendrocytes (OLs) are responsible for myelination in the CNS.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The two genotype groups (Stag2f/y;NesCre and Stag2f/y) had similar cellular compositions in scRNA-seq analysis.
source: As revealed by clusters in the t-SNE plot, the two genotype groups had similar cellular compositions (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: All cell clusters were present in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
source: All cell clusters were present in Stag2f/y;NesCre brains, again indicating generally normal neural cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: Stag2 ablation occurred early in the NPC stage and was maintained in all differentiated cell lineages.
source: Based on the expression changes of Stag2 and other cohesin genes in OLs, astrocytes, and neuronal lineages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D), it is clear that Stag2 ablation occurred early in the NPC stage and was maintained in all differentiated cell lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on scRNA-seq data showing Stag2 expression changes across cell types.

claim: There was a mild reduction in the proportion of MOLs in Stag2f/y;NesCre forebrains.
source: Quantification of the distributions of these five cell types within the OL lineage revealed a mild reduction in the proportion of MOLs in Stag2f/y forebrains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: More cells were present in the terminal maturation stages in the Stag2f/y brains.
source: The reclustering of single cells in the OL lineage along the pseudotime path revealed that more cells were present in the terminal maturation stages in the Stag2f/y brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: More cells were retained at the undifferentiated stages in the Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
source: Conversely, more cells were retained at the undifferentiated stages in the Stag2f/y;NesCre brains.
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis data.

claim: Some myelination genes, including Myelin and lymphocyte protein (Mal), were specifically repressed in Stag2f/y;NesCre MOLs.
source: Strikingly, some myelination genes, including Myelin and lymphocyte protein (Mal), were specifically repressed in Stag2f/y;NesCre MOLs, with their expression in nonneural cells unaltered (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: STAG2 deficiency delays the maturation of OLs.
source: These observations suggest that STAG2 deficiency delays the maturation of OLs and compromises myelination-specific gene expression in mature OLs.
evidence: This is an inference based on trajectory analysis and gene expression data.

claim: STAG2 deficiency compromises myelination-specific gene expression in mature OLs.
source: These observations suggest that STAG2 deficiency delays the maturation of OLs and compromises myelination-specific gene expression in mature OLs.
evidence: This is an inference based on scRNA-seq data showing reduced expression of myelination genes.

claim: Stag1 transcripts are less abundant in the OL lineage compared to Stag2 and genes encoding other cohesin core subunits, except for cycling OPCs.
source: Interestingly, compared to Stag2 and genes encoding other cohesin core subunits, Stag1 transcripts are less abundant in the OL lineage, except for cycling OPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C.

claim: The low expression of Stag1 in mature OLs might make these cells more dependent on Stag2 for function.
source: The low expression of Stag1 in mature OLs might make these cells more dependent on Stag2 for function.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of low Stag1 expression in mature OLs.

claim: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 271 genes were downregulated by more than two folds.
source: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 271 and 292 genes were downregulated or upregulated by more than two folds, respectively (Figure 4F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data of isolated primary OLs shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 292 genes were upregulated by more than two folds.
source: In Stag2-deleted OLs, 271 and 292 genes were downregulated or upregulated by more than two folds, respectively (Figure 4F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data of isolated primary OLs shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The downregulated genes in Stag2-deleted OLs were generally highly expressed in WT cells.
source: Intriguingly, the downregulated genes were generally highly expressed in WT cells, whereas the upregulated genes had low expression levels in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D.

claim: The upregulated genes in Stag2-deleted OLs had low expression levels in WT cells.
source: Intriguingly, the downregulated genes were generally highly expressed in WT cells, whereas the upregulated genes had low expression levels in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–D.

claim: The top pathways enriched in the downregulated DEGs in Stag2-deleted OLs included the cholesterol and small molecule biosynthetic pathways and oligodendrocyte differentiation.
source: The top pathways enriched in the downregulated DEGs included the cholesterol and small molecule biosynthetic pathways and oligodendrocyte differentiation (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Cilium organization and assembly are the top enriched pathways in the upregulated DEGs in Stag2-deleted OLs.
source: Cilium organization and assembly are the top enriched pathways in the upregulated DEGs (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs identified by RNA-seq analysis of the whole brain of Stag2-deficient mice, 42 were also differentially expressed in primary oligodendrocytes.
source: Among the 105 downregulated DEGs identified by RNA-seq analysis of the whole brain of Stag2-deficient mice, 42 were also differentially expressed in primary oligodendrocytes (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data from whole brain and isolated OLs shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Defective cholesterol biosynthesis and oligodendrocyte differentiation likely underly hypomyelination and neurological defects in Stag2 cKO mice.
source: Thus, defective cholesterol biosynthesis and oligodendrocyte differentiation likely underly hypomyelination and neurological defects in Stag2 cKO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathway analysis and gene expression data.

claim: Stag2 loss did not appreciably affect H3K27Ac enrichment at transcription start sites (TSSs).
source: We performed chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) experiments to examine the enrichment of the active transcription mark H3K27ac in Stag2f/y and Stag2f/y;NesCre OLs and found that Stag2 loss did not appreciably affect H3K27Ac enrichment at transcription start sites (TSSs) (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: The upregulated genes had much lower H3K27ac enrichment near their TSS, indicating that they were less active.
source: Consistent with our RNA-seq results, the upregulated genes had much lower H3K27ac enrichment near their TSS, indicating that they were less active.
evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP-seq data showing lower H3K27ac enrichment at upregulated genes.

claim: STAG2 was enriched at TSS of stable and downregulated genes, including genes in the cholesterol biosynthesis and myelination pathways.
source: Among other genomic loci, STAG2 was enriched at TSS of stable and downregulated genes, including genes in the cholesterol biosynthesis and myelination pathways (Figure 5C, D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by STAG2 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C, D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among the 271 downregulated DEGs, there were 210 genes (77%) with STAG2 enrichment near the transcriptional start site (TSS ± 2 kb).
source: Among the 271 downregulated DEGs, there were 210 genes (77%) with STAG2 enrichment near the transcriptional start site (TSS ± 2 kb).
evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: STAG2 occupied the promoter regions of many downregulated DEGs in oligodendrocytes.
source: Thus, STAG2 occupied the promoter regions of many downregulated DEGs in oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP-seq data showing STAG2 enrichment at promoters of downregulated genes.

claim: STAG2 was enriched at the TSS of upregulated genes to a lesser extent, with only 117 of the 292 (40%) upregulated DEGs exhibiting STAG2 ChIP-seq peaks at their TSS ± 2 kb regions.
source: It was enriched at the TSS of upregulated genes to a lesser extent, with only 117 of the 292 (40%) upregulated DEGs exhibiting STAG2 ChIP-seq peaks at their TSS ± 2 kb regions.
evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Stag2 loss might have indirectly affected the expression of less active genes.
source: Stag2 loss might have indirectly affected the expression of these less active genes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that upregulated genes have lower STAG2 binding.

claim: Few compartment switching events were observed in Stag2-deleted cells.
source: We observed few compartment switching events in Stag2-deleted cells (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Virtually all genomic regions in Stag2-deleted cells were kept in their original compartment categories (AA or BB).
source: Virtually all genomic regions in Stag2-deleted cells were kept in their original compartment categories (AA or BB) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: More genes located in the transcriptionally active A compartment (AA) were repressed in Stag2-deleted cells.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data, analysis of average gene expression changes of DEGs in these genomic regions revealed that more genes located in the transcriptionally active A compartment (AA) were repressed in Stag2-deleted cells and more genes in the transcriptionally silent B compartment (BB) were upregulated (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by integration of Hi-C and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: More genes in the transcriptionally silent B compartment (BB) were upregulated in Stag2-deleted cells.

claim: Genes that switched from the A compartment to the B compartment were not more repressed compared to those that remained in the A compartment.
source: Genes that switched from the A compartment to the B compartment were not more repressed compared to those that remained in the A compartment.

claim: Genes located in chromatin regions that switched from compartment B to A were not significantly activated compared to genes that stayed in the B compartment.

evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression changes in different compartment categories.

claim: Acute depletion of all forms of cohesin eliminates TAD formation.

claim: STAG1-cohesin compensates for the loss of STAG2-cohesin in spatial organization of chromatin at larger than megabase scales.
source: In contrast, deletion of Stag2 had minimal impact on TAD formation in oligodendrocytes (Figure 6E–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that STAG1-cohesin compensates for the loss of STAG2-cohesin in spatial organization of chromatin at larger than megabase scales.
